prompt.context: Your client is a large toy manufacturer named Marlin (think of a company such as Hasbro or Mattel) with $3B in sales. They are interested in potentially acquiring a smaller company named Dolphin which sells educational toys. Dolphin is different from Marlin since it employs a direct selling model. They hire independent contractors (ICs) to sell their toys for them: these ICs find people to hold parties for them, and invite about 8-10 people whom they sell these toys to. The ICs are paid 20% commission. If the ICs refer a friend to sell Dolphin products and that friend does so, that sale still generates 20% commission for the new IC, but also an additional, smaller commission for the person who originally referred them. This process continues and you get an increasingly smaller cut of sales from members referred by those you referred, etc. This downstream commission sums up to approximately 10% total. Dolphin has been losing revenues lately. Two years ago they had $35M in revenue, one year ago they had $28M, and this year they have $20M. This year they are operating at zero profitability — breakeven. Although the cost of the acquisition is not significant due to their relative sizes, Marlin wants to have a company that can pay its own way.
prompt.question: 1. What do both parties have to gain from this acquisition? 2. Why is Dolphin losing revenues and what can they do about it?

clarifying_info.q: Is the educational toy market growing?
clarifying_info.a: The educational toy market is growing at a rate of 3%; the overall toy market is flat.

clarifying_info.q: Are there new competitors in the educational toy space?
clarifying_info.a: There were no recent competitor entries in educational toys.

clarifying_info.q: How do competitors sell educational toys?
clarifying_info.a: Other educational toys are sold through retailers such as Target and Walmart. Dolphin is the only company currently selling educational toys with a direct sales model.

clarifying_info.q: Does Marlin currently sell educational toys?
clarifying_info.a: Marlin does not have any educational toys now, but other large toy manufacturers do.

clarifying_info.q: Is there demand for Dolphin's products?
clarifying_info.a: Dolphin products are in high demand. Many people complain that they cannot find a party when they want to. Price premium is expected for this selling model and people are willing to pay it.

clarifying_info.q: What is happening to the number of ICs?
clarifying_info.a: The number of ICs has been declining at 10%. Although ICs are being added, more ICs are leaving than joining.
Average party revenue remains constant at $200.
COGS = 50% of revenue, Fixed Costs = 20% of revenue, Selling Costs = IC commission + downstream commission.

exhibits.shows: A table comparing revenue, COGS, fixed costs, selling costs, total costs, and profit for the current year versus a scenario after the proposed commission change
exhibits.data: Before: Revenue $20M; After commission change: Revenue $40M (parties double). Structure includes rows for COGS, Fixed Costs, Selling Costs, Total Costs, and Profit.

framework: Question 1 — Strategic rationale for acquisition: (a) Revenue synergies, (b) Cost synergies, (c) Marlin's strategic position, (d) Educational toy industry dynamics
Question 2 — Root cause of Dolphin's revenue decline: (a) External factors (market, competition, pricing) vs. (b) Internal factors (sales force size, party frequency, compensation incentives)

questions.prompt: Question 1: What does each party gain from this acquisition?
questions.guidance: Revenue synergies: Dolphin gains access to Marlin's retail distribution channels (Target, Walmart), which could solve its distribution bottleneck since demand for its products is high. Marlin gains entry into the growing educational toy segment and brand loyalty benefits. Cost synergies: toys are made from similar physical materials, so shared manufacturing facilities and operational streamlining are possible. Strategic: Marlin improves competitive position relative to other large toy manufacturers who already have educational toys.

questions.prompt: Question 2a: Why is Dolphin losing revenue? Identify the root cause.
questions.guidance: Revenue decline is NOT driven by external factors: the educational toy market is growing at 3%, there are no new competitors, and Dolphin products are in high demand (people complain they cannot find a party). The decline is internal. Revenue = Number of ICs x Parties per IC x Revenue per party. Revenue per party is constant at $200. ICs are declining at 10%, but the total revenue decline exceeds 20% per year, so ICs must also be holding fewer parties each. Root cause: ICs are under-incentivized — Dolphin pays $40 per party (20% of $200) vs. industry average of $90 per party (30% of $300). ICs who work multiple jobs prefer to hold parties for competing products.

math.setup: Annual revenue decline: $35M → $28M → $20M. YoY decline: year 1 = ($35M-$28M)/$35M ≈ 20%; year 2 = ($28M-$20M)/$28M ≈ 29%. IC count declining at 10% does not fully explain >20% revenue decline, so parties per IC must also be falling. IC earnings: 20% commission x $200 avg party = $40/party. Industry benchmark: 30% x $300 = $90/party.
steps: Dolphin IC earnings per party = 20% x $200 = $40
Industry average earnings per party = 30% x $300 = $90
Gap = $90 - $40 = $50 per party; Dolphin ICs earn less than half the industry benchmark
math.answer: ICs are significantly under-compensated vs. industry, driving attrition and lower party frequency.

questions.prompt: Question 2b (math): Management proposes raising IC commission from 20% to 30% (keeping downstream at 10%), projecting that parties will double. Will this solve Dolphin's profitability problem?
questions.guidance: Candidate should build a before/after P&L using the given cost structure. At breakeven, costs = revenues = $20M. COGS = 50% of revenue. Fixed costs = 20% of revenue. Selling costs = IC commission + downstream. Before: selling = 30% x $20M = $6M. After: revenue doubles to $40M; COGS = 50% x $40M = $20M; fixed costs remain $4M (fixed); selling = 40% x $40M = $16M; total costs = $40M; profit = $0M. The commission increase does NOT improve profitability. Candidate should also note that 30% commission still trails the industry benchmark of 90/party vs. the new $60/party — so the doubling of parties is an optimistic assumption. Should explore further commission increases or alternative distribution channels.

math.setup: Cost structure: COGS = 50% of revenue, Fixed Costs = 20% of revenue (fixed in dollar terms at breakeven year levels), Selling Costs = (IC commission % + 10% downstream) x revenue. Current year is breakeven so total costs = $20M, giving: COGS = $10M, Fixed = $4M, Selling = $6M.
steps: Before: Revenue = $20M; COGS = 50% x $20M = $10M; Fixed = $4M; Selling = (20%+10%) x $20M = $6M; Total Costs = $20M; Profit = $0M
After (proposed): Revenue = $40M (parties double); COGS = 50% x $40M = $20M; Fixed = $4M (fixed); Selling = (30%+10%) x $40M = $16M; Total Costs = $40M; Profit = $0M
New IC earnings per party = 30% x $200 = $60 vs. industry $90 — still below benchmark, so doubling of parties is questionable
math.answer: Profit remains $0M after the commission change; the proposal does not improve profitability.

questions.prompt: Synthesis / revisiting Q1: How can Marlin and Dolphin help each other given Q2 findings?
questions.guidance: Dolphin's core problem is distribution bottleneck (too few ICs, under-incentivized). Marlin's retail distribution channels (Target, Walmart) provide an immediate alternative channel. Since demand is proven, Dolphin products should perform well in retail. This resolves Dolphin's profitability problem without relying solely on the difficult IC incentive fix. For Marlin: gains a growing product category, builds brand loyalty in educational toys, and strengthens competitive position vs. other large toy makers that already have educational lines. Cost synergies from shared manufacturing further improve the case.

brainstorming.prompt: What internal factors might explain why Dolphin is losing revenue?

categories.name: Sales force / distribution
ideas: Declining number of ICs — more leaving than joining
ICs holding fewer parties per period
ICs pursuing other direct-selling opportunities with higher commissions
Difficulty finding suitable areas or hosts for parties
Insufficient recruitment and onboarding of new ICs

categories.name: Compensation & incentives
ideas: IC commission of 20% ($40/party) far below industry average of 30% ($90/party)
Downstream referral commission structure may not incentivize recruitment sufficiently
Total seller earnings not competitive with alternative gig/direct-sales roles

categories.name: Product / pricing
ideas: Products may be outdated or less preferred (ruled out — high demand confirmed)
Prices too high for the format (ruled out — customers willing to pay premium)
Party format may feel outdated to younger demographic

categories.name: External factors (to consider and rule out)
ideas: Shift in preference away from party-based purchasing

recommendation: Marlin should proceed with the acquisition of Dolphin
The primary value driver is using Marlin's retail distribution (Target, Walmart) to immediately solve Dolphin's distribution bottleneck and restore revenue growth
Dolphin's proven consumer demand for educational toys gives Marlin an entry into a growing segment where competitors are already present
risks: The IC channel may continue to decline even post-acquisition if commission structure is not addressed, limiting the direct-sales business unit
Doubling of parties from a 30% commission increase is an optimistic assumption — actual recovery may be slower
Integration complexity between Marlin's retail-focused operations and Dolphin's direct-sales culture
Retail channel may cannibalize or undermine the premium/exclusivity positioning of the party-based model
next_steps: Pilot Dolphin products through a subset of Marlin's retail partners to validate demand at scale
Evaluate whether to maintain, restructure, or wind down the IC direct-sales model over time
Conduct full cost synergy analysis across manufacturing and supply chain
Assess competitive response from other educational toy manufacturers already in retail
